title: Workbench
text:
Note



The student-facing Workbench is a live Flask app on the FishView Mac mini (http://fishview.local:5052/workbench). This page documents the workflow so you can verify that the instructor walkthrough is consistent with what students actually see.



The two-step student workflow

Build your bundle — go to the FishView dashboard for your clade, review images for each species, mark exemplars with ★, then click Export Bundle. You receive a ZIP with the layout shown on the Home page.
Render a recipe against it — open the Workbench, upload your bundle ZIP plus any recipe .qmd from the Recipe Book (or your own), and click Render. The server unzips into bundle/, calls quarto    render, and returns the HTML + figures.



Pre-installed R packages on the Mac mini
ape          1.5-2x
phytools     3.x
pavo         2.x
geometry     0.5.x
scatterplot3d 0.3-x
tidyverse    2.x
ggtree       3.x
phyloseq     1.x       (used by a few advanced recipes)
nlme         3.x       (PGLS)
mvMORPH      1.x       (multivariate evolutionary models)
If you need a package that isn’t on this list, ask the TA — installation is trivial but requires SSH access.


Bundle layout the Workbench expects
bundle/
├── images/
│   └── <Genus_species>.png
├── <family>-tree.tre
├── picked_species.txt
├── picked_tip_labels.txt
└── README.txt
Recipes that use cached intermediates (e.g., pavo_classify.rds, phylo_pca.rds) seed those files on first render and use them on every subsequent render. The student doesn’t need to do anything special — the first knit is slow, every knit after that is fast.


Why the recipe code shows the pavo::classify call and the


readRDS call
Recipe fidelity. We want students to see the canonical pavo step (“here’s what generates the cluster centers”) even though the actual computation happened once. The pattern is:
# === Canonical call — runs once, then commented out ===
# classified <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(ann)), function(i) {
#   img <- pavo::getimg(file.path("bundle/images",
#                                 paste0(ann$species_dir[i], ".png")))
#   pavo::classify(img, kcols = ann$gestalt_k[i])
# })
# saveRDS(classified, "bundle/pavo_classify.rds")

classified <- readRDS("bundle/pavo_classify.rds")
The commented block stays in the rendered HTML (because Quarto echoes it by default) so students can read the call without paying its compute cost.


Common pitfalls

Cluster IDs reshuffle across machines. pavo::classify runs k-means internally and the cluster numbers are not stable across runs or packages. The species_k_bg.csv annotation must be regenerated if you re-classify from scratch on a different machine.
k must be ≥ 2. Some species look “monotone” but you still need k=2 (body + background) for the recipe to work; a few species with very uniform body colours produce NA on the chromatic boundary stats and drop out of the phyl.pca.
Tree tips don’t match species names. The student bundle pre-strips voucher suffixes (Chaetodon_auriga2 → Chaetodon_auriga) and drops duplicate tips. If you bring your own tree, you’ll need to do the same.
Pavo and tidyverse versions. Pin to the versions installed on the Mac mini. A pavo 2.x → 3.x bump changes the structure of the rimg attributes used in the gamut recipe.

title: Phylogeny with Traits — the Poster Hero Panel
text:
Tip



The visual hero of the poster. This recipe builds the centerpiece of Panel C (28” × 24” on the 48” × 36” layout): a ladderized chronogram with

branches colored by PhyloPC1 ancestral state,
tips = exemplar fish images + species names (every other by default),
five trait columns to the right of the tree: PC1, PC2, PC3, trophic level, body size (cm), each rendered as a filled circle whose color encodes the value.

Poster output. figures/phylogeny-with-traits-hero.pdf (28” × 24”). One self-contained PDF, no external legend assembly needed.



What you’re computing

Load the cached phylo_pca.rds for PC1–PC3 tip scores + the tree.
Load bundle/chaet_traits.csv for body size + trophic level (built by recipes/advanced/fetch_traits.R).
Run phytools::contMap on PC1 over the ladderized tree.
Plot with base graphics: tree on the left ~55% of canvas, then five circle-strip columns on the right.
Tip rendering: image + species name (every other tip shows an image; the rest show name only — controlled by show_every_n, default 2).
Image height auto-scales with n_tips so small trees get bigger icons. Formula: image_width_in = clamp(0.6 * sqrt(60 / n_tips),    0.25, 1.2).



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ape)
  library(phytools)
  library(png)
})

BUNDLE  <- "../../bundle"
FIGDIR  <- "../../figures"
dir.create(FIGDIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
IMG_DIR <- file.path(BUNDLE, "images")

read_fish_png <- function(path) {
  img <- readPNG(path)
  if (length(dim(img)) == 3) {
    if (dim(img)[3] == 3) {
      img <- array(c(img, rep(1, prod(dim(img)[1:2]))),
                   dim = c(dim(img)[1:2], 4))
    }
    mag <- img[,,1] > 0.8 & img[,,2] < 0.3 & img[,,3] > 0.8
    img[,,4][mag] <- 0
  }
  img
}



Load inputs

pp   <- readRDS(file.path(BUNDLE, "phylo_pca.rds"))
ppca <- pp$ppca
tree <- ladderize(pp$tree)   # ladderize NOW so node ordering is consistent

S    <- ppca$S
PC1  <- setNames(S[, 1], rownames(S))
PC2  <- setNames(S[, 2], rownames(S))
PC3  <- setNames(S[, 3], rownames(S))

traits <- read.csv(file.path(BUNDLE, "chaet_traits.csv"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Keep only species present in the tree
keep   <- intersect(tree$tip.label, traits$species)
tree   <- keep.tip(tree, keep)
traits <- traits[match(tree$tip.label, traits$species), ]
stopifnot(all(traits$species == tree$tip.label))
cat(sprintf("Tips with all data: %d\n", length(tree$tip.label)))

Tips with all data: 109

cat(sprintf("body_size_cm NAs:  %d\n",  sum(is.na(traits$body_size_cm))))

body_size_cm NAs:  0

cat(sprintf("trophic_level NAs: %d\n", sum(is.na(traits$trophic_level))))

trophic_level NAs: 0

n_sim <- sum(grepl("simulated", traits$source))
if (n_sim > 0) {
  message(sprintf("NOTE: %d species have at least one SIMULATED trait value (source contains 'simulated').", n_sim))
}

NOTE: 17 species have at least one SIMULATED trait value (source contains 'simulated').




PC1 ASR for branch coloring

cm1 <- contMap(tree, PC1, plot = FALSE, res = 200)
cm1 <- setMap(cm1, colors = c("#2c7bb6", "#abd9e9", "#ffffbf",
                              "#fdae61", "#d7191c"))



Color & size scales for the trait columns

# Diverging palette for PCs (signed values); sequential for the positive
# continuous traits.
div_pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#2c7bb6", "#abd9e9", "#ffffbf",
                              "#fdae61", "#d7191c"))(100)
seq_pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#f7fbff", "#c6dbef", "#6baed6",
                              "#2171b5", "#08306b"))(100)
warm_pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#fff5eb", "#fdd0a2", "#fd8d3c",
                               "#d94801", "#7f2704"))(100)

# Returns (col, cex) for a value within [vmin, vmax] under a given palette.
encode <- function(v, vmin, vmax, pal, min_cex = 0.45, max_cex = 1.45) {
  if (is.na(v)) return(list(col = "grey90", cex = min_cex, na = TRUE))
  v_clip <- pmin(pmax(v, vmin), vmax)
  idx    <- pmax(1, ceiling(100 * (v_clip - vmin) / (vmax - vmin)))
  cx     <- min_cex + (max_cex - min_cex) * (v_clip - vmin) / (vmax - vmin)
  list(col = pal[idx], cex = cx, na = FALSE)
}

# Pre-compute axis ranges so circles are comparable across the column.
rng_PC1  <- range(PC1, na.rm = TRUE)
rng_PC2  <- range(PC2, na.rm = TRUE)
rng_PC3  <- range(PC3, na.rm = TRUE)
# Symmetrize PC ranges around 0 so the diverging palette midpoint = 0.
sym <- function(r) { m <- max(abs(r)); c(-m, m) }
rng_PC1 <- sym(rng_PC1); rng_PC2 <- sym(rng_PC2); rng_PC3 <- sym(rng_PC3)

rng_tro  <- range(traits$trophic_level, na.rm = TRUE)
rng_bod  <- range(traits$body_size_cm,  na.rm = TRUE)



Plot helper


Code
plot_phylogeny_with_traits <- function(out_pdf,
                                       w = 28, h = 24,
                                       show_every_n = 2,
                                       legend_strip_h = 0.045) {

  n_tips <- length(tree$tip.label)
  total_h <- max(nodeHeights(tree))

  # Auto-image size (inches → data units after the plot is set up).
  image_width_in <- max(0.25, min(1.2, 0.6 * sqrt(60 / n_tips)))

  pdf(out_pdf, width = w, height = h)

  # Reserve right margin for the 5 trait columns + bottom strip for legends.
  # Note: contMap's plot() draws its own scalebar in the bottom-left if
  # legend != FALSE; we pass legend = total_h * 0.4 to keep it inside.
  par(bg = "white", mar = c(4.0, 0.4, 3.2, 22.0))
  plot(cm1,
       fsize   = 0, ftype = "off",
       lwd     = 1.5,
       outline = FALSE,
       legend  = total_h * 0.45,
       leg.txt = "PhyloPC1 (pattern density)",
       xlim    = c(0, total_h * 1.05))
  title("Chaetodontidae · phylogeny + color-pattern axes + ecology",
        line = 1.4, cex.main = 1.6, adj = 0)

  lpp   <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)
  tip_x <- lpp$xx[seq_len(n_tips)]
  tip_y <- lpp$yy[seq_len(n_tips)]

  # Per-row vertical spacing in data units.
  dy <- if (n_tips > 1) (max(tip_y) - min(tip_y)) / (n_tips - 1) else 1

  # Convert image width from inches to data units (rough — uses panel width).
  panel_in_w  <- w - sum(par("mai")[c(2, 4)])     # plot inches width
  data_per_in <- total_h * 1.05 / panel_in_w
  img_w_data  <- image_width_in * data_per_in
  img_h_data  <- dy * 0.85

  # x-anchor for tip glyphs
  x_glyph <- max(tip_x) + total_h * 0.012

  # Render tip rows
  for (i in seq_len(n_tips)) {
    sp  <- tree$tip.label[i]
    y_c <- tip_y[i]
    show_image <- ((i - 1) %% show_every_n == 0)
    png_path <- file.path(IMG_DIR, paste0(sp, ".png"))
    if (show_image && file.exists(png_path)) {
      img <- read_fish_png(png_path)
      rasterImage(img,
                  xleft   = x_glyph,
                  xright  = x_glyph + img_w_data,
                  ybottom = y_c - img_h_data / 2,
                  ytop    = y_c + img_h_data / 2)
      text(x_glyph + img_w_data / 2, y_c - img_h_data / 2 - dy * 0.18,
           gsub("_", " ", sp),
           adj = c(0.5, 1.0), cex = 0.55, font = 3, col = "grey15")
    } else {
      text(x_glyph, y_c, gsub("_", " ", sp),
           adj = c(0, 0.5), cex = 0.55, font = 3, col = "grey15")
    }
  }

  # ------ Trait circle columns -----------------------------------------
  # Lay out columns to the RIGHT of the image strip, in inches → data units.
  col_start_in <- image_width_in + 0.20   # gap after image
  col_w_in     <- 0.55                    # per-column width
  col_gap_in   <- 0.08
  col_total_in <- col_w_in + col_gap_in
  col_x_data   <- function(j) {
    x_glyph + img_w_data + (col_start_in + (j - 0.5) * col_total_in) * data_per_in
  }
  col_labels  <- c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "Trophic", "Body (cm)")
  col_pals    <- list(div_pal, div_pal, div_pal, warm_pal, seq_pal)
  col_ranges  <- list(rng_PC1, rng_PC2, rng_PC3, rng_tro, rng_bod)
  col_values  <- list(
    PC1[tree$tip.label],
    PC2[tree$tip.label],
    PC3[tree$tip.label],
    traits$trophic_level,
    traits$body_size_cm
  )

  # Header row for the columns
  header_y <- max(tip_y) + dy * 1.8
  for (j in seq_along(col_labels)) {
    text(col_x_data(j), header_y, col_labels[j],
         adj = c(0.5, 0.5), cex = 1.0, font = 2, col = "grey20")
  }

  # Circle rows
  for (j in seq_along(col_labels)) {
    v_all  <- col_values[[j]]
    rng    <- col_ranges[[j]]
    pal    <- col_pals[[j]]
    xc     <- col_x_data(j)
    for (i in seq_len(n_tips)) {
      enc <- encode(v_all[i], rng[1], rng[2], pal)
      points(xc, tip_y[i], pch = 21,
             bg = enc$col,
             col = if (enc$na) "grey60" else "grey25",
             cex = enc$cex * 1.6, lwd = 0.4)
    }
  }

  # Per-column compact legend strip across the bottom-right margin
  legend_y <- min(tip_y) - dy * 4
  for (j in seq_along(col_labels)) {
    xc  <- col_x_data(j)
    rng <- col_ranges[[j]]
    pal <- col_pals[[j]]
    # 5-step colorbar drawn as 5 small squares stacked vertically
    n_steps <- 5
    sw <- col_w_in * data_per_in * 0.4
    sh <- dy * 0.35
    for (k in seq_len(n_steps)) {
      val <- rng[1] + (k - 0.5) / n_steps * (rng[2] - rng[1])
      idx <- pmax(1, ceiling(100 * (val - rng[1]) / (rng[2] - rng[1])))
      rect(xc - sw / 2,
           legend_y - sh * (n_steps - k),
           xc + sw / 2,
           legend_y - sh * (n_steps - k - 1),
           col = pal[idx], border = "grey40", lwd = 0.3)
    }
    text(xc, legend_y + sh * 0.4,
         sprintf("%.2g", rng[2]), adj = c(0.5, 0), cex = 0.55, col = "grey25")
    text(xc, legend_y - sh * n_steps - sh * 0.3,
         sprintf("%.2g", rng[1]), adj = c(0.5, 1), cex = 0.55, col = "grey25")
  }

  # Provenance note in bottom-left
  mtext(sprintf("n = %d species  ·  PC scores from cached phyl.pca (BM, corr)  ·  body & trophic: rfishbase v%s  ·  depth (not shown): xlsx layered",
                n_tips, packageVersion("rfishbase")),
        side = 1, line = 2.6, cex = 0.65, col = "grey35", adj = 0)

  dev.off()
  invisible(out_pdf)
}




Hero PDF (28” × 24”, matches Panel C)

plot_phylogeny_with_traits(hero_pdf, w = 28, h = 24, show_every_n = 2)

title: Color Gamut (Foundation Recipe)
text:
Tip



Foundation Recipe — every group runs this one. The output is a single number (gamut volume) plus a 3D RGB scatter showing where the clade lives in color space.



What you’re computing
For each exemplar species:

pavo::classify(img, kcols = k) quantizes the image into k perceptual color clusters (one of those clusters is the background).
We pull the cluster centers out as RGB triples (the per-species “palette”).
We drop the background cluster (recorded in bg_class_id from the pavo adjacency CSV).
Pool all surviving cluster centers across the clade → a cloud of points in the unit RGB cube.
Gamut volume = 3D convex hull of that cloud (via geometry::convhulln), expressed as a fraction of the unit cube (1 = fills the full RGB space).



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(pavo)
  library(geometry)
  library(scatterplot3d)
})

Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'tibble' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'purrr' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.2

BUNDLE <- "../../bundle"

# Per-species annotation: gestalt_k (used for classify) and bg_class_id
# (cluster index to treat as background). In a real student workflow, you
# would build this file by inspecting your classified images.
ann <- read.csv(file.path(BUNDLE, "species_k_bg.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bg  <- setNames(ann$bg_class_id, ann$species_dir)



The pavo classify step

# === Canonical recipe call — RUN ONCE, then comment out ===
# This takes ~10-15 minutes on a Mac mini for 130 species.
# After it completes, the saveRDS line below caches the result so the
# rest of the recipe (and every re-render) runs in seconds.

classified <- vector("list", nrow(ann))
names(classified) <- ann$species
for (i in seq_len(nrow(ann))) {
  png <- file.path(BUNDLE, "images", paste0(ann$species_dir[i], ".png"))
  img <- pavo::getimg(png)
  set.seed(20260526)   # stable cluster IDs across knits
  classified[[i]] <- pavo::classify(img, kcols = ann$gestalt_k[i])
}
saveRDS(classified, file.path(BUNDLE, "pavo_classify.rds"))


# Cached object produced by the chunk above (live call commented out).
classified <- readRDS(file.path(BUNDLE, "pavo_classify.rds"))
cat(sprintf("Loaded %d classified images from cache.\n", length(classified)))

Loaded 130 classified images from cache.




Extract cluster centers (drop background)

get_palette <- function(rimg_obj, bg_id) {
  rgb_mat <- attr(rimg_obj, "classRGB")           # k × 3 matrix
  if (is.null(rgb_mat)) return(NULL)
  if (!is.na(bg_id) && bg_id >= 1 && bg_id <= nrow(rgb_mat)) {
    rgb_mat <- rgb_mat[-bg_id, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  rgb_mat
}

palettes <- mapply(
  function(rimg_obj, sp) {
    p <- get_palette(rimg_obj, bg[gsub(" ", "_", sp)])
    if (is.null(p)) return(NULL)
    data.frame(species = sp, R = p[, "R"], G = p[, "G"], B = p[, "B"])
  },
  classified, names(classified),
  SIMPLIFY = FALSE
)
palettes <- bind_rows(palettes)
cat(sprintf("Palette cloud: %d cluster centers from %d species\n",
            nrow(palettes), length(unique(palettes$species))))

Palette cloud: 341 cluster centers from 130 species

4   Amphichaetodon melbae 0.497675267 0.542690550 0.47387326

The gamut volume

pts <- as.matrix(palettes[, c("R", "G", "B")])
hull <- convhulln(pts, options = "FA")
vol <- hull$vol
cat(sprintf("Chaetodontidae gamut volume: %.4f of unit RGB cube (%.1f%%)\n",
            vol, 100 * vol))

Chaetodontidae gamut volume: 0.1715 of unit RGB cube (17.1%)




Plot — the gamut as a Stoddard-style faceted hull
The classic Stoddard & Prum (2011) tetrahedral-color-space figures show the achieved color volume as a semi-transparent faceted polyhedron, with the hull’s triangular facets visible against a wireframe reference space. We do the same here in RGB space: the unit cube is the theoretical maximum, the faceted polyhedron is what Chaetodontidae actually occupies.

# Hull triangulation — the same `hull` object computed above already has
# the triangle vertex indices in its $hull slot (options="FA").
triangles <- hull$hull
cols <- rgb(pts[, 1], pts[, 2], pts[, 3])

# Draw the unit RGB cube wireframe + scatter, then overlay hull facets
par(bg = "white", mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
s3d <- scatterplot3d(NA, NA, NA,
                     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), zlim = c(0, 1),
                     xlab = "R", ylab = "G", zlab = "B",
                     box = FALSE, grid = FALSE, angle = 35,
                     main = sprintf("Chaetodontidae gamut (volume = %.3f, %.1f%% of RGB cube)",
                                    vol, 100 * vol))

Warning in min(x): no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf


Warning in max(x): no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf

# Reference: unit-cube wireframe (12 edges)
cube_v <- expand.grid(R = c(0, 1), G = c(0, 1), B = c(0, 1))
cube_edges <- list(
  c(1, 2), c(3, 4), c(5, 6), c(7, 8),   # R-axis edges
  c(1, 3), c(2, 4), c(5, 7), c(6, 8),   # G-axis edges
  c(1, 5), c(2, 6), c(3, 7), c(4, 8)    # B-axis edges
)
for (e in cube_edges) {
  p1 <- s3d$xyz.convert(cube_v$R[e[1]], cube_v$G[e[1]], cube_v$B[e[1]])
  p2 <- s3d$xyz.convert(cube_v$R[e[2]], cube_v$G[e[2]], cube_v$B[e[2]])
  segments(p1$x, p1$y, p2$x, p2$y, col = "grey80", lwd = 0.8)
}

# Hull facets — order back-to-front by mean B (rough depth-sort so front
# facets paint over back ones)
facet_depth <- apply(triangles, 1, function(idx) mean(pts[idx, 3]))
order_idx   <- order(facet_depth)

for (i in order_idx) {
  v <- triangles[i, ]
  facet_pts <- pts[v, ]
  facet_col <- rgb(mean(facet_pts[, 1]),
                   mean(facet_pts[, 2]),
                   mean(facet_pts[, 3]),
                   alpha = 0.35)
  scr <- s3d$xyz.convert(facet_pts[, 1], facet_pts[, 2], facet_pts[, 3])
  polygon(scr$x, scr$y, col = facet_col, border = "grey25", lwd = 0.4)
}

# Cluster centers on top
scr_pts <- s3d$xyz.convert(pts[, 1], pts[, 2], pts[, 3])
points(scr_pts$x, scr_pts$y, col = cols, pch = 16, cex = 1.3)
points(scr_pts$x, scr_pts$y, col = "grey15", pch = 1, cex = 1.3, lwd = 0.5)

# Light per-axis labels back on
axis_labels <- c("R", "G", "B")
for (j in seq_along(axis_labels)) {
  pos <- c(0, 0, 0); pos[j] <- 1
  p <- s3d$xyz.convert(pos[1], pos[2], pos[3])

text:
Note










Field
Content




Species in tree
109 (one tip per species, voucher suffixes stripped)


Exemplars in bundle
130 (some species have no tip; some tips have no exemplar)


Family size
~130 species in ~12 genera


Crown age
~43 Ma (Eocene)


Sexual system
Gonochoristic; long-term pair bonds in many Chaetodon


Primary diet
Obligate corallivory, generalist invertivory, planktivory — often within the same genus


Depth range
Reef crest to lower mesophotic (~150 m in Prognathodes)


Key references
Bellwood et al. (2010); Cowman et al. (2017); Hemingson & Bellwood (2018); Hodge et al. (2014)







Chaetodontidae is a family of small reef-associated percomorphs distributed across tropical Indo-Pacific, Atlantic, and Eastern Pacific reefs. The current working classification recognizes ~130 species in two subfamilies — the Chaetodontinae (Chaetodon and allies, ~90 species) and the Prognathodinae (Prognathodes, Roa, and the Forcipiger / Hemitaurichthys group). The phylogenomic tree used in this walkthrough contains 109 tips after collapsing voucher duplicates, with a crown age of ~43 Ma fixed by congruification onto a fossil-calibrated reference tree.
The most recent backbone work places butterflyfishes as sister to pomacanthids (Bellwood et al., 2010; Cowman et al., 2017), with which they share many of the perceptual and signaling features explored in this course. Generic boundaries within Chaetodon remain partly unsettled, but the broad species-group structure (e.g., the trifascialis, unimaculatus, citrinellus, and kleinii groups) is well supported.



Butterflyfishes are diurnal, visually oriented reef specialists. Most species are obligately coral-associated, and ~60% of Chaetodon are obligate corallivores that feed primarily on the tissue of living scleractinians (Cole et al., 2008). The remaining species are generalist invertivores (Forcipiger, Chelmon) or midwater planktivores (Hemitaurichthys, several Heniochus and Prognathodes). Diet matters for color biology because corallivores tend to maintain extremely tight site fidelity around their feeding territories, where mate choice and species recognition both operate against the same visual backdrop.
A defining life-history feature of the family is long-term pair bonding: many Chaetodon species form monogamous pairs that persist for years and coordinate territorial defense and feeding (Hodge et al., 2014). Both sexes look essentially identical (sexual monochromatism) but the pair, treated as a perceptual unit, is highly distinctive against the reef — which has shaped the family’s iconic bold, contrastive patterns.



Hemingson & Bellwood (2018) used the butterflyfishes as their flagship system for studying color pattern divergence in sympatric sister pairs, finding that sister species in geographic overlap diverge more in pattern than those in allopatry, especially on metrics related to stripe orientation and boundary geometry. This effect motivates the metrics computed in the Color Gamut and Continuous ASR recipes on this site.
Pattern diversity within the family spans:

Vertical-bar designs (Chaetodon trifasciatus, C. lunulatus, C. ornatissimus) where the body is divided into 3-7 contrasting bands.
Horizontal-stripe designs (C. striatus, C. octofasciatus) where bars are rotated 90° to align with the body axis.
Spot-and-eyespot designs (C. punctatofasciatus, C. semeion, C. unimaculatus) with discrete pigmented dots and false eyespots near the caudal peduncle.
Bicolour wedge designs (C. paucifasciatus, C. mertensii) with the body sharply divided into anterior pale and posterior coloured halves.
Cryptic and pelagic designs (Hemitaurichthys polylepis, H. zoster) for the planktivorous and offshore taxa.

The gamut built in the next recipe will sample the full RGB range present across these patterns, after removing background pixels.

title: PGLS — Color PCs vs Ecology
text:
Tip



Advanced recipe. Asks: after controlling for phylogeny, do the leading color-pattern axes (PC1, PC2) covary with ecology (trophic level) and morphology (body size)? Fits two phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) models with a Brownian + λ correlation structure (nlme::corPagel), then makes a 2×2 grid of partial-residual scatter plots (one per predictor per response).
Poster output. figures/pgls-color-traits-hero.pdf — 12” × 24” portrait, drops into Panel D of the 48”×36” template.



What you’re computing
For each color-pattern PC (PC1, PC2):

Build a tip-aligned data frame with: PC, trophic_level, body_size_cm.
Drop species missing either covariate.
Fit gls(PC ~ trophic_level + body_size_cm,               correlation = corPagel(1, tree, fixed = FALSE),               method = "ML").
Extract the partial-residual y-values for each covariate (i.e., what’s left in the response after removing the effect of the other covariate, on the original data scale).
Plot each partial-residual scatter with a fitted line + λ + p in the corner. No big stats table — annotations only.



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ape)
  library(nlme)
  library(phytools)
})

BUNDLE <- "../../bundle"
FIGDIR <- "../../figures"
dir.create(FIGDIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)



Load inputs

pp   <- readRDS(file.path(BUNDLE, "phylo_pca.rds"))
tree <- pp$tree
S    <- pp$ppca$S

PC1  <- setNames(S[, 1], rownames(S))
PC2  <- setNames(S[, 2], rownames(S))

traits <- read.csv(file.path(BUNDLE, "chaet_traits.csv"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
df <- data.frame(species = tree$tip.label,
                 PC1 = PC1[tree$tip.label],
                 PC2 = PC2[tree$tip.label])
df <- merge(df, traits[, c("species", "body_size_cm", "trophic_level",
                           "source")],
            by = "species", all.x = TRUE)
df <- df[match(tree$tip.label, df$species), ]
stopifnot(all(df$species == tree$tip.label))

# Log-transform body size (length traits are right-skewed).
df$log_body <- log(df$body_size_cm)

# Drop rows missing covariates (PGLS requires complete cases).
keep <- complete.cases(df[, c("PC1", "PC2", "log_body", "trophic_level")])
df_use   <- df[keep, ]
tree_use <- keep.tip(tree, df_use$species)
rownames(df_use) <- df_use$species
cat(sprintf("Species used in PGLS: %d (dropped %d for missing covariates)\n",
            nrow(df_use), sum(!keep)))

Species used in PGLS: 109 (dropped 0 for missing covariates)

n_sim <- sum(grepl("simulated", df_use$source))
if (n_sim > 0) {
  message(sprintf("NOTE: %d species in the PGLS sample have at least one SIMULATED trait value.", n_sim))
}

NOTE: 17 species in the PGLS sample have at least one SIMULATED trait value.




Fit the two PGLS models

fit_pgls <- function(response_col) {
  f <- as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ trophic_level + log_body", response_col))
  # Try several starting values for lambda; nlme + corPagel is fragile when
  # the unconstrained optimum sits near the [0, 1] boundary.
  starts <- c(0.5, 0.9, 0.1, 0.99, 0.0)
  ctrl   <- nlme::glsControl(opt = "optim", maxIter = 200, msMaxIter = 200,
                             tolerance = 1e-6, msTol = 1e-6)
  for (lam0 in starts) {
    m <- tryCatch(
      nlme::gls(f, data = df_use,
                correlation = ape::corPagel(lam0, tree_use,
                                             form = ~species,
                                             fixed = FALSE),
                method = "ML",
                control = ctrl),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (!is.null(m)) {
      attr(m, "fit_note") <- sprintf("converged from lambda start = %.2f", lam0)
      return(m)
    }
  }
  # Last resort: pure Brownian (lambda fixed at 1)
  m <- nlme::gls(f, data = df_use,
                 correlation = ape::corPagel(1, tree_use,
                                              form = ~species,
                                              fixed = TRUE),
                 method = "ML",
                 control = ctrl)
  attr(m, "fit_note") <- "Pagel optimizer failed; reverted to fixed lambda = 1 (Brownian)"
  m
}

m_pc2 <- fit_pgls("PC2")

extract_stats <- function(m) {
  s    <- summary(m)
  tt   <- s$tTable
  lam  <- tryCatch(
    as.numeric(coef(m$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
  if (length(lam) == 0) lam <- 1.0   # fixed-lambda fit
  list(
    coef = tt[, "Value"],
    se   = tt[, "Std.Error"],
    p    = tt[, "p-value"],
    lambda = lam
  )
}

Partial-residual computation

# Partial residuals: response minus the contribution of "other" predictors,
# plus the contribution of the focal predictor (so the fitted line passes
# through the cloud at the focal-predictor slope). On the original scale of
# the response.
pr_data <- function(m, focal, response_col) {
  b <- coef(m)
  fitted_other <- 0
  for (term in setdiff(names(b), c("(Intercept)", focal))) {
    fitted_other <- fitted_other + b[term] * df_use[[term]]
  }
  y_partial <- df_use[[response_col]] - fitted_other
  data.frame(species = df_use$species,
             x = df_use[[focal]],

}

plot_panel <- function(pr, focal_label, response_label, m, focal_term,
                       xlab = focal_label) {
  par(mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 2.4, 1.0), bg = "white")
  cols <- clade_color(pr$species)
  plot(pr$x, pr$y,
       pch = 21, bg = cols, col = "grey20",
       cex = 1.4, lwd = 0.4,
       xlab = xlab,
       ylab = sprintf("%s (partial)", response_label),
       cex.lab = 1.15, cex.axis = 1.0, las = 1,
       main = sprintf("%s vs %s", response_label, focal_label),
       cex.main = 1.25, font.main = 2)
  grid(col = "grey92")
  # Fitted line: slope = PGLS coef on focal_term, intercept anchored to
  # mean of partial residuals.
  b <- coef(m)
  slope <- b[focal_term]
  x_seq <- seq(min(pr$x), max(pr$x), length.out = 50)
  y_seq <- slope * (x_seq - mean(pr$x)) + mean(pr$y)
  lines(x_seq, y_seq, col = "black", lwd = 2)

  # Annotation in upper-right
  s   <- summary(m)
  tt  <- s$tTable
  lam <- tryCatch(
    as.numeric(coef(m$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
  if (length(lam) == 0) lam <- 1.0   # fixed-lambda fit
  txt <- c(
    sprintf("coef = %+.3f", tt[focal_term, "Value"]),
    sprintf("SE   = %.3f",   tt[focal_term, "Std.Error"]),
    sprintf("p    = %s",     format.pval(tt[focal_term, "p-value"], digits = 2)),
    sprintf("λ    = %.2f",   lam)
  )
  usr <- par("usr")
  text(usr[2] - diff(usr[1:2]) * 0.02, usr[4] - diff(usr[3:4]) * 0.04,
       paste(txt, collapse = "\n"),
       adj = c(1, 1), cex = 0.85, family = "mono",
       col = "grey15")
}

Interpretation

PC1 (pattern density) — if trophic_level has a significant positive coefficient, more-carnivorous species tend toward simpler patterns after accounting for body size and phylogeny. A negative coefficient flips the sign. The body-size coefficient tells you whether larger species converge on simple patterns (positive) or busy patterns (negative), again controlling for diet and phylogeny.
PC2 (color diversity) — the same logic, with the response now being chromatic richness.
λ ≈ 1: trait residuals are strongly phylogenetically structured (Brownian). λ ≈ 0: residuals look independent across species; the ordinary GLS without correction would have given the same answer.
Wide bands of colored points clustering together in any panel indicate one genus is doing most of the work — a flag to re-run the same model within that genus to check for Simpson’s paradox.

title: Phylomorphospace — PC1 × PC2
text:
Tip



Elective recipe. Takes the cached phyl.pca from the bundle and projects all species into PC1 × PC2, then connects them through their reconstructed internal nodes (the classic Sidlauskas / phytools “phylomorphospace”). Each tip is plotted as the species’ exemplar image rather than a dot, so the morphospace itself shows the patterns the PCs are measuring.
Poster output. figures/phylomorphospace-PC1-PC2-hero.pdf — 12” × 9”, drops directly into Panel B of the 48”×36” template.



What you’re computing

Load the cached phylogenetic PCA (phylo_pca.rds) — same object the continuous-asr recipe uses, so PC scores are comparable across the two recipes.
Pull S (n species × n PCs) and keep columns 1 and 2.
Estimate internal-node positions in PC1×PC2 with phytools::fastAnc (one ancestral-state reconstruction per axis under Brownian motion).
Plot each tip as its exemplar PNG (head-left, auto-sized by tree size) and draw the phylogenetic edges connecting tips through internal nodes.
Annotate the corner with variance explained and the top pavo-metric loadings per axis (no big table on the figure — that goes in the methods sidebar of the poster).



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ape)
  library(phytools)
  library(png)
})

BUNDLE  <- "../../bundle"
FIGDIR  <- "../../figures"
dir.create(FIGDIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
IMG_DIR <- file.path(BUNDLE, "images")

# Helper: read PNG and make magenta background transparent
read_fish_png <- function(path) {
  img <- readPNG(path)
  if (length(dim(img)) == 3) {
    if (dim(img)[3] == 3) {
      img <- array(c(img, rep(1, prod(dim(img)[1:2]))),
                   dim = c(dim(img)[1:2], 4))
    }
    mag <- img[,,1] > 0.8 & img[,,2] < 0.3 & img[,,3] > 0.8
    img[,,4][mag] <- 0
  }
  img
}



Load cached PCA + tree

pp   <- readRDS(file.path(BUNDLE, "phylo_pca.rds"))
ppca <- pp$ppca
tree <- pp$tree

S    <- ppca$S
PC1  <- setNames(S[, 1], rownames(S))
PC2  <- setNames(S[, 2], rownames(S))

eig  <- diag(ppca$Eval)
ve   <- 100 * eig / sum(eig)

cat(sprintf("Tips with PC scores: %d\n", length(PC1)))

Top loadings per axis

rownames(loadings) <- pp$stat_cols

top_loaders <- function(v, k = 3) {
  ord <- order(abs(v), decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(k)]
  paste0(names(v)[ord],
         sprintf("(%+.2f)", v[ord]),

Reconstruct internal-node positions

# Brownian ASR for each axis using fastAnc (same generative model as
# phyl.pca, so this is the consistent way to project ancestors).
anc1 <- fastAnc(tree, PC1)
anc2 <- fastAnc(tree, PC2)

# Combine tip + node coords into a single (n_tips + n_nodes) × 2 matrix,
# indexed by phylo's node numbering (tips 1..ntip, internals ntip+1..ntip+nnode).
n_tips <- length(tree$tip.label)
coords <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_tips + tree$Nnode, ncol = 2,
                 dimnames = list(NULL, c("PC1", "PC2")))
coords[1:n_tips, 1] <- PC1[tree$tip.label]
coords[1:n_tips, 2] <- PC2[tree$tip.label]
coords[(n_tips + 1):nrow(coords), 1] <- anc1[as.character((n_tips + 1):(n_tips + tree$Nnode))]
coords[(n_tips + 1):nrow(coords), 2] <- anc2[as.character((n_tips + 1):(n_tips + tree$Nnode))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(coords))



Auto-size the tip images
The image width scales as sqrt(60 / n_tips) so a small tree gets large icons and a big tree gets small icons; clamped to a sane range. With 109 tips the formula gives roughly 0.44” per image on a 12”-wide canvas, which prints as a recognizable thumbnail at 48”-poster scale.

n_species <- length(tree$tip.label)

# image_width_in is the on-PDF image width in INCHES; we convert to PC1-axis
# units below using the data range.
image_width_in <- max(0.25, min(1.2, 0.6 * sqrt(60 / n_species)))
cat(sprintf("n_species = %d  →  image_width_in = %.3f in\n",
            n_species, image_width_in))

plot_pms <- function(out_pdf, w = 12, h = 9,
                     image_width_in = 0.44,
                     edge_col = "grey55", edge_lwd = 0.6,
                     bg_col = "white", border_col = "grey15",
                     point_fallback_col = "#1f77b4") {

  # Data ranges with a 12% pad so images near the edge don't get clipped.
  pad <- 0.12
  xr <- range(coords[, 1]); xr <- xr + diff(xr) * c(-pad, pad)
  yr <- range(coords[, 2]); yr <- yr + diff(yr) * c(-pad, pad)

  # Convert image width in inches to data units (PC1).
  # plot area width ≈ canvas width minus margins. Use a 70% effective ratio,
  # i.e., reserve 30% for margins.
  data_per_inch_x <- diff(xr) / (w * 0.70)
  data_per_inch_y <- diff(yr) / (h * 0.70)
  img_w_data <- image_width_in * data_per_inch_x
  img_h_data <- image_width_in * data_per_inch_y * 0.65  # fish are wider than tall

  pdf(out_pdf, width = w, height = h)
  par(bg = bg_col, mar = c(4.4, 4.4, 3.0, 1.2))
  plot(NA, NA, xlim = xr, ylim = yr,
       xlab = sprintf("PhyloPC1  (%.1f%% var)", ve[1]),
       ylab = sprintf("PhyloPC2  (%.1f%% var)", ve[2]),
       cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.0, las = 1,
       main = "Chaetodontidae phylomorphospace · PC1 × PC2",
       font.main = 2, cex.main = 1.25)
  grid(col = "grey90", lty = "dotted")

  # Phylo edges first, so images paint over them.
  for (e in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) {
    p <- tree$edge[e, 1]; c <- tree$edge[e, 2]
    segments(coords[p, 1], coords[p, 2],
             coords[c, 1], coords[c, 2],
             col = edge_col, lwd = edge_lwd)
  }
  # Internal nodes as small filled circles for visual continuity.
  internal <- (n_tips + 1):nrow(coords)
  points(coords[internal, 1], coords[internal, 2],
         pch = 21, bg = "grey85", col = "grey45", cex = 0.55, lwd = 0.4)

  # Tip images
  for (i in seq_len(n_tips)) {
    sp <- tree$tip.label[i]
    png_path <- file.path(IMG_DIR, paste0(sp, ".png"))
    x <- coords[i, 1]; y <- coords[i, 2]
    if (file.exists(png_path)) {
      img <- read_fish_png(png_path)
      rasterImage(img,
                  xleft   = x - img_w_data / 2,
                  xright  = x + img_w_data / 2,
                  ybottom = y - img_h_data / 2,
                  ytop    = y + img_h_data / 2)
    } else {
      points(x, y, pch = 21, bg = point_fallback_col,
             col = border_col, cex = 1.4)
    }
  }

  # Corner annotation — small, NO big table.
  ann <- c(sprintf("PC1: %.1f%% var | top loaders: %s", ve[1], pc1_top),
           sprintf("PC2: %.1f%% var | top loaders: %s", ve[2], pc2_top),
           sprintf("n = %d species; internal nodes via fastAnc (BM)", n_species))
  legend("topright", legend = ann, bty = "n",
         cex = 0.72, text.col = "grey25")

  dev.off()
  invisible(out_pdf)
}

Reading the plot

Tips that sit far from the centroid have extreme color-pattern signatures on whatever the leading axes are (here: pattern density and color diversity).
Long thin edges = lineages that have moved a lot in morphospace per Ma; short edges connecting nearby points = stasis.
Crossing edges are typical and expected — phylomorphospace projects a high-dimensional Brownian process onto 2 axes, so apparent crossings in PC1×PC2 don’t violate phylogenetic constraints.
Cluster regions of similar-looking fish images = convergence on the leading pattern axes.



How to extend

Color edges by clade: assign each edge a color based on the genus of its descendant tip (cheap heuristic since most edges sit within one genus in a 109-tip family tree).
Layer environmental data: shade the background of the plot by the Brownian-reconstructed value of a co-evolving trait (e.g., depth).

Plot helper — tree + image tips + species names
The helper plots a contMap, suppresses the default tip labels, and instead places (a) the exemplar image at each tip and (b) a small italic species name underneath the image. It writes both a PNG (for HTML preview) and a hero PDF (for poster insertion).


Code
plot_pc_with_tips <- function(cm, ttl, hero_pdf,
                              img_pad = 0.05, lbl_pad = 0.014,
                              img_height_frac = 0.85,
                              w = 14, h = 32) {

  tip_labels <- cm$tree$tip.label
  n_tips     <- length(tip_labels)
  total_h    <- max(nodeHeights(cm$tree))

  draw_one <- function(scale_for_pdf = TRUE) {
    par(mar = c(3.0, 0.4, 2.6, 9.0), bg = "white")
    plot(cm,
         fsize    = 0,            # suppress default tip labels
         ftype    = "off",
         lwd      = 1.4,
         outline  = FALSE,
         legend   = total_h * 0.55,
         leg.txt  = "",
         xlim     = c(0, total_h * 1.45))
    title(ttl, line = 1.0, cex.main = 1.4)

    # Tip y-coords from phytools last-plot info
    lpp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)
    tip_x <- lpp$xx[seq_len(n_tips)]
    tip_y <- lpp$yy[seq_len(n_tips)]

    # Image extent: width set by total_h * img_pad; height set by
    # img_height_frac of the vertical spacing between adjacent tips.
    dy <- if (n_tips > 1) (max(tip_y) - min(tip_y)) / (n_tips - 1) else 1
    img_h <- dy * img_height_frac
    img_w <- total_h * img_pad

    lbl_cex <- if (scale_for_pdf) 0.62 else 0.55

    for (i in seq_len(n_tips)) {
      sp  <- tip_labels[i]
      png_path <- file.path(IMG_DIR, paste0(sp, ".png"))
      x0  <- tip_x[i] + total_h * 0.005
      y_c <- tip_y[i]
      if (file.exists(png_path)) {
        img <- readPNG(png_path)
        rasterImage(img,
                    xleft   = x0,
                    xright  = x0 + img_w,
                    ybottom = y_c - img_h / 2,
                    ytop    = y_c + img_h / 2)
      }
      text(x0 + img_w + total_h * lbl_pad, y_c,
           gsub("_", " ", sp),
           adj = c(0, 0.5),
           cex = lbl_cex,
           font = 3, col = "grey15")
    }
  }

  # Hero PDF
  pdf(hero_pdf, width = w, height = h)
  draw_one(scale_for_pdf = TRUE)
  dev.off()

  # In-document version (will be captured by the chunk fig settings)
  draw_one(scale_for_pdf = FALSE)
  invisible(NULL)
}

top_branches <- function(cm, br, k = 10) {
  tr  <- cm$tree
  ord <- order(br, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(k)]
  descendants <- sapply(ord, function(e) {
    child <- tr$edge[e, 2]
    if (child <= length(tr$tip.label)) {
      tr$tip.label[child]

    rank        = seq_len(k),
    rate        = round(br[ord], 4),
    edge_length = round(tr$edge.length[ord], 2),
    descendant  = descendants
  )
}

title: Phylogenetic Signal — Blomberg’s K
text:
Tip



Core recipe. Tests whether closely related butterflyfishes share similar color patterns using Blomberg’s K and Pagel’s lambda on the six core pavo adjacency metrics plus the first three phyloPCA axes. K < 1 means color evolves faster than Brownian drift; K > 1 means it is phylogenetically conserved.
Poster outputs. A summary table of K and lambda values plus a contMap of PC1 for visual context, exported as figures/signal-summary-table.pdf and figures/signal-contmap-pc1.pdf.



What you’re computing

Blomberg’s K for each of the six core pavo variables (m, A, Jc, Jt, m_dS, m_dL) plus PhyloPC1–PC3.
Pagel’s lambda for the same variables (a complementary signal metric).
A contMap of PC1 painted onto the chronogram to visualize the signal.



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({

  library(phytools)
  library(knitr)
  library(kableExtra)
})

                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

S    <- ppca$S

# Normalize species names

# Core pavo variables

# Intersect tree and pavo data

cat(sprintf("Species in common: %d\n", length(shared)))

Blomberg’s K for pavo variables

K_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(0),
  K        = numeric(0),
  p_value  = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE

for (v in pavo_vars) {

  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  overlap <- intersect(names(x), tree_k$tip.label)
  if (length(overlap) < 10) {
    cat(sprintf("Skipping %s — only %d species with data\n", v, length(overlap)))
    next

  t_sub <- keep.tip(tree_k, overlap)
  x <- x[t_sub$tip.label]
  res <- phylosig(t_sub, x, method = "K", test = TRUE, nsim = 999)
  K_results <- rbind(K_results, data.frame(
    Variable = v,
    K        = round(res$K, 4),
    p_value  = round(res$P, 4),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

Tip

title: Measurement Robustness
text:
Tip



Core recipe. Monte Carlo perturbation test: adds realistic measurement noise (estimated from multi-image error SDs) to every species’ pavo values 200 times and recomputes Blomberg’s K each time. If the observed K sits above the noise distribution, the signal is real.
Poster outputs. figures/mc-robustness-K.pdf — boxplot of MC K distributions with observed K overlaid as red diamonds.



Setup

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ape)
  library(phytools)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
  library(kableExtra)
})

Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.2

Load data

                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tree <- read.tree(file.path(BUNDLE, "chaetodontidae-tree.tre"))
tree <- ladderize(tree)
pavo$species <- gsub(" ", "_", pavo$species)

pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
shared <- intersect(pavo$species, tree$tip.label)
pavo   <- pavo[match(shared, pavo$species), ]
tree_mc <- keep.tip(tree, shared)

# Build trait matrix
trait_mat <- as.matrix(pavo[, pavo_vars])
rownames(trait_mat) <- pavo$species

# Drop incomplete rows
complete <- complete.cases(trait_mat)
trait_mat <- trait_mat[complete, ]
tree_mc   <- keep.tip(tree_mc, rownames(trait_mat))
trait_mat <- trait_mat[tree_mc$tip.label, ]

cat(sprintf("MC analysis on %d species x %d variables\n",
            nrow(trait_mat), ncol(trait_mat)))

MC analysis on 109 species x 6 variables




Define error SDs
These are representative measurement error standard deviations estimated from multi-image measurements of butterflyfish exemplars. In the student workflow, each group measures their own error species in Demo 8.

error_sd <- c(
  m    = 0.015,
  A    = 0.08,
  Jc   = 0.04,
  Jt   = 0.03,
  m_dS = 0.02,
  m_dL = 0.03
)
cat("Error SDs used:\n")

Error SDs used:

print(error_sd)

    m     A    Jc    Jt  m_dS  m_dL 
0.015 0.080 0.040 0.030 0.020 0.030 




Monte Carlo loop

set.seed(2026)
n_iter <- 200

K_mc <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_iter, ncol = length(pavo_vars),
               dimnames = list(NULL, pavo_vars))

for (iter in seq_len(n_iter)) {
  noisy <- trait_mat
  for (v in pavo_vars) {
    noisy[, v] <- trait_mat[, v] + rnorm(nrow(trait_mat), 0, error_sd[v])
  }
  for (v in pavo_vars) {
    x <- setNames(noisy[, v], rownames(noisy))
    K_mc[iter, v] <- tryCatch(
      phylosig(tree_mc, x, method = "K"),
      error = function(e) NA
    )
  }
}
cat(sprintf("Completed %d MC iterations\n", n_iter))

Completed 200 MC iterations




Observed K values

obs_K <- sapply(pavo_vars, function(v) {
  x <- setNames(trait_mat[, v], rownames(trait_mat))
  phylosig(tree_mc, x, method = "K")
})

  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", color = "grey50", outlier.size = 0.8) +

  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +

fit_pgls <- function(response, predictor, df, tree) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(response, "~", predictor))
  starts <- c(0.5, 0.9, 0.1, 0.99, 0.01)
  ctrl <- glsControl(opt = "optim", maxIter = 200, msMaxIter = 200)
  for (lam0 in starts) {
    m <- tryCatch(
      gls(f, data = df,
          correlation = corPagel(lam0, tree, form = ~species, fixed = FALSE),
          method = "ML", control = ctrl),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m)) return(m)
  }
  gls(f, data = df,
      correlation = corPagel(1, tree, form = ~species, fixed = TRUE),
      method = "ML", control = ctrl)
}

extract_lambda <- function(m) {
  tryCatch(
    as.numeric(coef(m$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) 1.0)
}

fit_pgls <- function(response, predictor, df, tree) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(response, "~", predictor))
  starts <- c(0.5, 0.9, 0.1, 0.99, 0.01)
  ctrl <- glsControl(opt = "optim", maxIter = 200, msMaxIter = 200)
  for (lam0 in starts) {
    m <- tryCatch(
      gls(f, data = df,
          correlation = corPagel(lam0, tree, form = ~species, fixed = FALSE),
          method = "ML", control = ctrl),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m)) return(m)
  }
  gls(f, data = df,
      correlation = corPagel(1, tree, form = ~species, fixed = TRUE),
      method = "ML", control = ctrl)
}

extract_lambda <- function(m) {
  tryCatch(
    as.numeric(coef(m$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) 1.0)
}

Tip



Pattern recipe. Tests the character displacement hypothesis using 33 sister pairs from the chaets-divergence project. For each pair, Mahalanobis distance in the 6-dimensional pavo color-pattern space quantifies how different their color patterns are. fit_pgls_cat <- function(response, df, tree) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(response, "~ region_group"))
  starts <- c(0.5, 0.9, 0.1, 0.99, 0.01)
  ctrl <- glsControl(opt = "optim", maxIter = 200, msMaxIter = 200)
  for (lam0 in starts) {
    m <- tryCatch(
      gls(f, data = df,
          correlation = corPagel(lam0, tree, form = ~species, fixed = FALSE),
          method = "ML", control = ctrl),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m)) return(m)
  }
  gls(f, data = df,
      correlation = corPagel(1, tree, form = ~species, fixed = TRUE),
      method = "ML", control = ctrl)
}

extract_lambda <- function(m) {
  tryCatch(
    as.numeric(coef(m$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) 1.0)
}

Interpretation
Chaetodontidae are predominantly Indo-Pacific, with a handful of Atlantic endemics (Prognathodes + a few Caribbean Chaetodon). The 8-region coding from BioGeoBEARS allows a finer decomposition than the binary Atlantic/Indo-Pacific split used in simpler analyses.
If the omnibus PGLS F-test is significant for PC1, it indicates that pattern complexity differs across ocean basins after controlling for phylogeny. Atlantic Prognathodes tend to be deep-water, less colorful species, which may drive a region effect on PC2 (color diversity).
The ordination overlay reveals whether region-based clusters emerge in color space, or whether phylogenetic history dominates the pattern (i.e., closely related species are near each other regardless of region). A strong region signal after phylogenetic correction would suggest convergent evolution of color phenotypes within basins.
